figures.title: Array insertion: make a gap
figures.description: Shift the suffix before writing the new value into the live array.
figures.keyIdea: Move the suffix right to left before writing the new value. Otherwise an unread value can be overwritten.

figures.title: Unlinking a known list node
figures.description: Bypass the middle node in both directions, then clear its links.
figures.keyIdea: Repair both neighbors, then detach the removed node. A forward link and its backward link must agree.

figures.title: Stack: last in, first out
figures.description: Push and pop share the top; the newest value leaves first.
figures.keyIdea: The top is the final live array element. Appending and removing there gives last-in, first-out order.

figures.title: Queue wrap: slots versus order
figures.description: The head moves around the buffer while FIFO order stays intact.
figures.keyIdea: At logical offset i, use (head + i) % capacity. Dequeue follows logical order, never raw slot order.

figures.title: Hash collisions: keep both keys
figures.description: Equal hash codes select one bucket; key equality still decides a match.
figures.keyIdea: A shared hash only selects a bucket. Equality still distinguishes the mappings; a collision must preserve both.

figures.title: LRU: a hit changes the order
figures.description: Promote a cache hit before deciding which entry to evict next.
figures.keyIdea: A hit changes recency. On overflow, evict the left end; the map points straight to the node to move.

figures.title: AVL rotation
figures.description: Inserting 30, 20 and 10 produces a left-heavy chain. A right rotation makes 20 the root with children 10 and 30, preserving in-order traversal and restoring height one.
figures.keyIdea: Rotate links, preserve sorted order, and restore the height balance.

figures.title: Heap: array and tree
figures.description: Bottom-up heapify turns 9,4,7,1,3,2 into the array 1,3,2,4,9,7. The matching complete binary tree labels every zero-based array slot and keeps every parent no greater than its children.
figures.keyIdea: A heap puts the minimum at its root; the array is not globally sorted.

figures.title: Trie: preserve shared prefixes
figures.description: The words car, cart and cat share a c-a prefix. Deleting car clears the r node's word marker but preserves its t child for cart and the sibling t branch for cat.
figures.keyIdea: Deleting a word clears its end marker. Keep nodes still needed by longer words.

figures.title: Union-find components
figures.description: Union operations on five indices produce components {0,1,2} and {3,4}. Parent arrows point toward roots 0 and 3, whose component sizes are three and two. Finding index 2 follows its link to root 0.
figures.keyIdea: Connectivity is a partition: five indices form two disjoint components.

figures.title: Fenwick prefix blocks
figures.description: For values 2,-1,4,3, one-based Fenwick slots cover [0,1), [0,2), [2,3) and [0,4). The prefix ending at zero-based boundary 3 combines slots 3 and 2: 4+1=5.
figures.keyIdea: A prefix query combines disjoint blocks. The low bit gives each block's length.

figures.title: Segment minimum
figures.description: An interval tree over 8,3,7,5 answers the minimum on [1,4) by combining leaf [1,2) with node [2,4). Replacing index 1 with 9 repairs its ancestors and changes the query answer from 3 to 5. Leaves use power-of-two padding with MAX_VALUE when needed.
figures.keyIdea: Each node covers an adjacent interval. A point set repairs one path to the root.

figures.title: Binary search: lower bound
figures.description: Half-open ranges find the first target among duplicate values.
figures.keyIdea: Keep the first possible index inside [low, high]. A value at least the target moves high left, so duplicates cannot hide the first match.

figures.title: Merge sort: split and combine
figures.description: Split into singletons, then merge sorted children bottom up.
figures.keyIdea: Each parent merges two sorted children. A level costs O(n) work, and there are O(log n) levels: O(n log n) overall.

figures.title: Quicksort: three-way partition
figures.description: Gather duplicate pivot values into one finished equal region.
figures.keyIdea: Only the smaller and greater regions recurse. Equal keys already belong together, so the equal region needs no further sorting.

figures.title: Coin change: build an optimum
figures.description: Compare every final coin; the largest-first greedy choice loses.
figures.keyIdea: best[a] is optimal for exactly amount a. Each candidate adds one coin to a solved, strictly smaller amount.

figures.title: 0/1 knapsack: sweep backward
figures.description: Sweep capacities backward so an item cannot reuse itself.
figures.keyIdea: Descending capacity keeps the current item out of its own predecessor states. Each item is used at most once.

figures.title: KMP: keep the overlap
figures.description: Prefix fallback retains the overlap between two pattern matches.
figures.keyIdea: After a match, retain the longest matched suffix that is also a pattern prefix. This preserves overlapping matches without rescanning text.

figures.title: N-queens: reject and undo
figures.description: Trace failed placements before reaching the first valid board.
figures.keyIdea: Place one queen per row. Reject used columns or diagonals; undo an unsuccessful choice before trying another.

figures.title: Greedy: finish first
figures.description: Choose earliest finishing intervals; touching endpoints remain compatible.
figures.keyIdea: The earliest finishing compatible activity leaves at least as much time for everything that follows. This maximizes the count, not total duration.

figures.title: Bubble sort: adjacent swaps
figures.description: Swap neighboring values; each pass settles a maximum on the right.
figures.keyIdea: Each adjacent comparison moves the larger value right. After a pass, the unsorted range's maximum is fixed at its end; a swap-free pass stops.

figures.title: BFS: discovered vs processed
figures.description: Follow the queue separately from discovery; isolate unreachable vertex 5.
figures.keyIdea: Discovery happens on enqueue, before processing; isolated vertices stay unreachable.

figures.title: Dijkstra: distance and path
figures.description: Compare weighted routes from source 0 and distinguish unreachable vertex 4.
figures.keyIdea: Choose the cheapest weighted path; absence is separate from every numeric distance.

figures.title: Negative edge or cycle?
figures.description: A negative edge yields -3; an added cycle makes targets 1 and 2 unbounded.
figures.keyIdea: A negative edge can be safe; this API rejects any reachable negative cycle.

figures.title: SCCs and bridges differ
figures.description: Directed return paths form SCCs; undirected essential edges are bridges.
figures.keyIdea: SCCs test directed mutual reachability; bridges test an undirected edge's necessity.

figures.title: Compare growth, not timings
figures.description: Five illustrative functions share a value of one at input size one. A logarithmic work axis shows logarithmic, linear, n log n, quadratic and exponential growth without implying benchmark timings.
figures.keyIdea: Theoretical normalized work; constants, machines and measured runtime are outside this comparison.

figures.title: Articulation points
figures.description: A bowtie graph of two triangles sharing vertex 2 is searched depth-first from 0 with discovery and low values shown, and removing vertex 2 leaves the separate components {0, 1} and {3, 4}.
figures.keyIdea: An articulation point has a child whose low is at least its own disc.

figures.title: Bipartite or odd cycle
figures.description: A 6-cycle splits into left {0, 2, 4} and right {1, 3, 5}, while a 5-cycle with a tail has an edge 2-3 joining two vertices of the same colour, and the witness is the odd cycle 2, 1, 0, 4, 3.
figures.keyIdea: A graph is two-colourable exactly when it has no odd cycle; the first edge joining equal colours exposes one.

figures.title: Euler path
figures.description: A square with a diagonal and a pendant edge has odd degree only at vertices 0 and 4, so the Euler path starts at 0 and walks every edge once: 0, 1, 2, 3, 0, 2, 4.
figures.keyIdea: Connected edges with zero or two odd-degree vertices give an Euler path.

figures.title: Kruskal and Prim
figures.description: One weighted graph on five vertices has a minimum spanning tree of total weight 11. Kruskal keeps edges in the order 1, 2, 3, 5 and skips two that close a cycle, while Prim from vertex 0 picks 1, 2, 5, 3.
figures.keyIdea: Both algorithms add cheapest safe edges, in different orders, to reach one total.

figures.title: Maximum flow and minimum cut
figures.description: A four-vertex flow network from source 0 to sink 3 carries a maximum flow of 5. The source side {0, 1} is the set reachable in the residual graph, and the three edges leaving it have capacities 2, 1 and 2, summing to 5.
figures.keyIdea: Edges leaving the final source side are saturated and sum to the flow.

figures.title: Augmenting a matching
figures.description: A bipartite matching of size 2 leaves left vertex 1 and right vertex 1 free. Flipping the alternating path L1, R0, L0, R1 gives the maximum matching of size 3.
figures.keyIdea: Flipping one augmenting path grows a matching by exactly one pair.

figures.title: Binary lifting for LCA
figures.description: In a seven-vertex tree rooted at 0, lca(6, 4) lifts vertex 6 by 2 to vertex 3, finds the 2^2 and 2^1 ancestors equal, jumps both vertices by 2^0 to 1 and 2, and returns their parent 0, read from the table of 2^j-th ancestors.
figures.keyIdea: Equalise depths, then jump both by powers of two while ancestors differ.

figures.title: Tree diameter by two sweeps
figures.description: In a seven-vertex tree, a breadth-first sweep from vertex 0 ends farthest at 6, and a second sweep from 6 ends farthest at 5, so the path 6, 3, 1, 0, 2, 5 of 5 edges is a longest path.
figures.keyIdea: A sweep from any vertex ends at a diameter endpoint; sweep again from there.

figures.title: From hash code to slot
figures.description: Integer keys 65536 and 131072 have hash codes 0x00010000 and 0x00020000, whose low four bits are both 0, so a plain mask sends both to slot 0. Spreading with h ^ (h >>> 16) and multiplying by 0x9E3779B9 gives slots 1 and 2 of 16.
figures.keyIdea: Mixing lets high bits pick the slot, so such keys stop colliding.

figures.title: Probing past a taken slot
figures.description: In an 8-slot table holding K, B and G, put(L) finds home slot 7 taken by G, wraps to slot 0 and stores L there; get(T), also homed at 7, visits slots 7, 0 and 1 and stops at the empty slot 1.
figures.keyIdea: A collision moves to the next slot and wraps past the end; a lookup retraces it to the first empty slot.

figures.title: Backward-shift deletion
figures.description: In the cluster C, H, M, B at slots 3 to 6, clearing only H's slot 4 would hide M, which is stored at slot 5 but starts its search at slot 4. Backward-shift deletion moves M to slot 4, clears slot 5 and leaves B at its home slot 6.
figures.keyIdea: Shifting later keys back keeps every key reachable.

figures.title: LFU frequency buckets
figures.description: A capacity-3 LfuCache after put A, B, C and get C holds A and B in bucket 1 and C in bucket 2. get(B) moves B to the end of bucket 2, and put(D) then evicts A, the oldest key of bucket 1.
figures.keyIdea: Hits lift keys; the oldest key in the lowest bucket is evicted.

figures.title: Bloom filter bits
figures.description: A 16-bit Bloom filter with two probes per key sets bits 8, 11, 1 and 3 for apple and pear. kiwi reads bits 8 and 7 and bit 7 is clear, a definite miss; plum reads bits 1 and 11, both set, a false positive.
figures.keyIdea: One clear bit proves absence; all-set bits mean only possibly present.

figures.title: Count-Min rows
figures.description: A Count-Min sketch of 3 rows by 8 columns after adding apple 3, pear 1, fig 2, plum 4 and kiwi 1. pear reads counters 2, 3 and 1 in its three rows, and the minimum, 1, is the estimate.
figures.keyIdea: Rows only overcount, so a key's smallest counter is its estimate.

figures.title: Heap sift paths
figures.description: In the min heap 1, 3, 8, 4, 5, 9, add(7) appends at slot 6 and swaps up one level to slot 2, giving 1, 3, 7, 4, 5, 9, 8. remove() then takes out 1, moves 8 to the root and sifts it down two levels to slot 3, giving 3, 4, 7, 8, 5, 9.
figures.keyIdea: Each repair follows one path of at most log2 n levels.

figures.title: Top k with a bounded heap
figures.description: Selection.smallestK over the stream 8, 3, 9, 5, 2, 5, 1 with k = 3 fills the heap with 8, 3, 9, then evicts 9, evicts 8, drops the second 5 and evicts 5 for 1, ending with 1, 2, 3.
figures.keyIdea: The root is the largest value kept; an arrival must beat it to get in.

figures.title: Trie prefix walk
figures.description: For the words car, card, care, cart, cat and dog, wordsWithPrefix("ca", 3) walks the c and a nodes, then emits car, card and care in sorted order and stops before cart and cat; the dog branch is never visited.
figures.keyIdea: Walk the prefix once, then visit children in sorted order until the limit.

figures.title: Sparse table overlap
figures.description: For the values 5, 2, 6, 4, 7, 3, 8, 1, rangeMin(1, 7) takes the minimum of the blocks [1, 5) and [3, 7), which overlap on indices 3 and 4, and gets 2. A sum of the same blocks would give 41 instead of 30.
figures.keyIdea: Minimum ignores the overlap of two blocks; a sum would count it twice.

figures.title: Lazy range add
figures.description: In a LazySegmentTree over 1, 2, 3, 4, rangeAdd(2, 4, 5) stops at the node covering [2, 4), raising its sum to 17 and leaving a pending +5 for its leaves. rangeSum(3, 4) then reads the leaf's stored 4, adds the pending 5 and returns 9.
figures.keyIdea: A range add stops at a covering node and leaves a pending value.

figures.title: Path compression
figures.description: In a UnionFind over 9 indices, union(0, 5) hangs the size-4 root 4 under the size-5 root 0. Before find(7) the path is 7, 6, 4, 0; afterwards 7 and 6 point directly at 0.
figures.keyIdea: Union by size keeps trees shallow; find re-points its path at the root.

figures.title: Appending to a full array
figures.description: A DynamicArray with capacity 4 holds 10, 20, 30 and 40, so add(50) allocates 8 slots, copies the four values and writes 50 at index 4. That append copies 4 values; the next copy happens at append 9 and moves 8, for 12 copies in 9 appends.
figures.keyIdea: Doubling makes copies rare: n appends copy fewer than 2n values in total, so one append costs O(1) amortized.

figures.title: Insert after a known node
figures.description: In the chain 10, 20, 30, inserting 15 after 10 takes two link writes: 15.next = 10.next, then 10.next = 15, giving 10, 15, 20, 30. Writing 10.next = 15 first makes 15.next point at 15 itself and leaves 20 and 30 unreachable.
figures.keyIdea: Link the new node onward first, then redirect the predecessor.

figures.title: Matching brackets with a stack
figures.description: An ArrayStack traces {[()]}: three pushes and three pops leave it empty. The same stack traced on ([)] holds ( and [ when the closer ) arrives, and the top [ does not match it, so the string is rejected at the third character.
figures.keyIdea: The stack holds exactly the unmatched openers; a closer must match the top.

figures.title: A deque at both ends
figures.description: A RingDeque with four slots receives addLast(20), addLast(30), addFirst(10) and addLast(40); addFirst moves the head from slot 0 back to slot 3, and the tail ends at slot 2. removeLast() returns 40 and removeFirst() returns 10, leaving 20 and 30.
figures.keyIdea: Both ends are indices on a circular buffer: addFirst steps the head back and wraps.

figures.title: Reaching index 5
figures.description: In a DynamicArray of eight values, get(5) reads slot 5 in one jump. In a DoublyLinkedList of the same values it starts at the tail and follows 2 links, because 5 is in the back half; the hop counts for indices 0 to 7 are 0, 1, 2, 3, 3, 2, 1 and 0.
figures.keyIdea: An array reaches any index in one jump; a list walks links from the nearer end.

figures.title: Euclid and back-substitution
figures.description: NumberTheory.gcd(240, 46) divides 240 by 46, 46 by 10, 10 by 6, 6 by 4 and 4 by 2, reaching remainder 0, so the gcd is 2. Substituting the divisions backwards gives 2 = 47 times 46 minus 9 times 240, the coefficients of extendedGcd.
figures.keyIdea: The last nonzero remainder is the gcd, and undoing each division writes it as x×a + y×b.

figures.title: modPow by repeated squaring
figures.description: NumberTheory.modPow(3, 13, 1000) reads the bits of 13 = 1101 from the lowest: the squares of 3 are 3, 9, 81 and 561 modulo 1000, and the result 3, 3, 243, 323 changes only on the 1 bits, ending at 323.
figures.keyIdea: Square the base once per exponent bit and multiply it in only for 1 bits: O(log e) steps.

figures.title: Sieve of Eratosthenes
figures.description: NumberTheory.primesUpTo(30) on a grid of 1 to 30: 2 crosses out 14 multiples from 4, 3 crosses out 4 more from 9, 5 crosses out 25, and the ten numbers never crossed are the primes 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, 17, 19, 23 and 29.
figures.keyIdea: A prime p starts crossing at p×p, because smaller multiples have a smaller prime factor.

figures.title: Reservoir sampling
figures.description: Sampling.reservoirSample over the items A to H with k = 3 and seed 17 fills the reservoir with A, B, C, then draws j for each later arrival with replacement chance 3/4 down to 3/8; D, F and H replace slots 0, 0 and 1, giving F, H, C.
figures.keyIdea: Arrival i is kept with chance k/i, so every item seen so far ends up in the sample with equal chance.

figures.title: Alias table columns
figures.description: AliasTable for the weights 1, 1, 2, 4 has four equal columns: A and B each keep half their column and give the other half to D, while C and D fill their columns. Adding the pieces back gives the probabilities 1/8, 1/8, 1/4 and 1/2.
figures.keyIdea: Equal columns split between two items let one uniform column pick and one coin flip draw any weight.

figures.title: A set as a bit mask
figures.description: The set {1, 3} of four elements is the int mask 1010 = 10. Testing bit 3 gives 1, setting bit 2 gives 1110, clearing bit 3 gives 0010, and (sub - 1) & mask walks the subsets 10, 8, 2 and 0.
figures.keyIdea: A set is an int: test, set and clear bits in one operation, and (sub − 1) & mask visits every subset.

figures.title: LCS table and traceback
figures.description: The longest-common-subsequence table for GCTA and TGCAT, with the path longestCommonSubsequence walks back from the corner: it goes up on the tie at the corner, takes T, C and G on equal letters, and returns GCT.
figures.keyIdea: The traceback re-derives each choice from the table: take equal letters, otherwise move toward the larger neighbour, and go up on a tie.

figures.title: Edit distance path
figures.description: The edit-distance table for brain and paint with the path editScript returns: delete b, replace r with p, keep a, i and n, then insert t, for distance 3.
figures.keyIdea: Walking back from the corner prefers the diagonal, then delete, then insert; each step that is not a match adds 1.

figures.title: Matrix chain splits
figures.description: The cost table for four matrices with dimensions 30, 1, 40, 10, 25, the three candidate splits of the whole chain, and the stored splits that give (A1((A2A3)A4)) at cost 1400.
figures.keyIdea: Each cell keeps the cheapest split k; following the stored splits from the whole chain down gives the parenthesization.

figures.title: Held-Karp states
figures.description: The Held-Karp table for four cities, one cost per visited set and last city, the closing edge back to city 0, and the optimal tour 0, 2, 3, 1, 0 of cost 80.
figures.keyIdea: Held-Karp keeps one best cost per (visited set, last city), so 2^n n^2 steps replace the (n-1)! tours.

figures.title: Weighted interval choices
figures.description: Four weighted intervals sorted by end with their last compatible interval, the take-or-skip comparison for each, and the walk back that chooses B and D for total weight 10.
figures.keyIdea: Take an interval only if its weight plus the best earlier compatible schedule beats skipping it.

figures.title: Huffman merges and lengths
figures.description: Five symbols with frequencies 5, 9, 12, 13 and 16 are merged two lightest at a time into a tree, which gives code lengths 3, 3, 2, 2 and 2 and a weighted length of 124.
figures.keyIdea: Merging the two lightest nodes first leaves the rarest symbols deepest, so frequent symbols get the shortest codes.

figures.title: Subset sum, two halves
figures.description: Six values are split into two halves of three; the sums of all eight subsets of each half are listed, and the first right sum whose complement is stored on the left selects indices 0, 1 and 3 for target 6.
figures.keyIdea: Each half has only 2^(n/2) subsets, so storing one half's sums and scanning the other's finds a pair in about 2^(n/2) steps, not 2^n.

figures.title: Three ways to store a graph
figures.description: One directed graph with 4 vertices and the edges 0 to 1, 0 to 2, 2 to 1 and 2 to 3, shown as an adjacency list, a 4 by 4 adjacency matrix and an edge list, each with the cost of testing an edge and listing neighbors.
figures.keyIdea: Edge tests favor a matrix; neighbor scans favor an adjacency list.

figures.title: BFS and DFS visit order
figures.description: A 6-vertex undirected graph from source 0: breadthFirst visits 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 in layers of distance 0, 1 and 2, while depthFirst visits 0, 1, 3, 4, 5, 2 by following one branch to its end.
figures.keyIdea: A queue visits whole layers; a stack follows one branch to its end.

figures.title: Kahn's topological order
figures.description: Kahn's algorithm on a 5-vertex DAG whose in-degrees are 2, 1, 0, 0 and 2: it pops ready vertices 2, 3, 0, 1, 4, lowering in-degrees and refilling the ready queue, and outputs 2, 3, 0, 1, 4.
figures.keyIdea: A vertex is output once its in-degree is 0, so every edge points forward.

figures.title: Shortest-path chooser
figures.description: A column of seven yes-or-no questions from all pairs, unweighted, 0-1 weights, DAG, negative weights and heuristic to nonnegative weights, each paired with the algorithm and the repository method that answers it.
figures.keyIdea: Use the most specific algorithm whose precondition your graph meets; each one exploits a fact the general one cannot assume.

figures.title: 0-1 BFS and its deque
figures.description: 0-1 BFS from vertex 0 on a 4-vertex directed graph: weight-0 targets are pushed to the front of the deque and weight-1 targets to the back, so vertex 1 is first queued at distance 1 and then improved to 0 through 0, 2, 3, 1.
figures.keyIdea: Zero-weight edges go to the deque's front, unit-weight edges to its back.

figures.title: A* with a good heuristic
figures.description: A* on a 5 by 5 unit grid from cell 10 to cell 14 with the Manhattan heuristic: the route 10, 11, 12, 13, 14 has f = g + h equal to 4 everywhere, the heuristic was called for 13 of 25 cells, and with h = 0 it was called for 21.
figures.keyIdea: A good heuristic keeps the search near the route; far cells never get an h evaluation.

figures.title: One Floyd-Warshall round
figures.description: A 4-vertex directed graph: allowing vertex 1 as a stop-over improves the distance matrix entry d[0][2] from 9 to 5 because d[0][1] + d[1][2] = 3 + 2, and no other entry changes.
figures.keyIdea: Round k asks whether going through vertex k beats the best route so far.

figures.title: Two pointers, sorted array
figures.description: pairWithSum on 1, 2, 3, 4, 6 with target 6 starts at the two ends: 1 + 6 is too large so the right index drops, 1 + 4 is too small so the left index drops, and 2 + 4 matches at indices 1 and 3.
figures.keyIdea: Each move drops an index with no partner: at most n - 1 moves.

figures.title: Window jumping a repeat
figures.description: longestSubstringWithoutRepeats on abcbad grows the window to abc, jumps its start to index 2 when b repeats, ignores the stale earlier a at index 0, and ends with the longest window cbad at indices 2 to 5.
figures.keyIdea: The left edge never moves back, so each unit is added once: linear time.

figures.title: Next greater by stack
figures.description: nextGreaterIndices on 2, 1, 2, 4, 3 keeps unresolved indices on a stack: index 1 is resolved by the second 2, the equal 2 at index 0 stays, and the 4 resolves indices 2 and 0, giving 3, 2, 3, -1, -1.
figures.keyIdea: Each index is pushed once and popped once: O(n) despite the inner loop.

figures.title: Range adds by differences
figures.description: applyRangeAdds on five zeros marks +3 at index 1 and -3 at index 4, then +2 at index 0 and -2 at index 2, and one running sum produces 2, 5, 3, 3, 0.
figures.keyIdea: Two marks per update, then one running sum: O(n + u) in total.

figures.title: Sweeping events for rooms
figures.description: minimumMeetingRooms on the intervals [1, 4), [2, 5), [5, 7) and [6, 8) sorts the eight start and end events, processes the end at 5 before the start at 5, and reaches a depth of 2, so two rooms suffice.
figures.keyIdea: The busiest moment sets the room count; at a tie an end comes first.

figures.title: Inversions during a merge
figures.description: countInversions on 2, 4, 1, 3, 5 merges the sorted halves 2, 4 and 1, 3, 5: emitting 1 jumps over two left values, emitting 3 jumps over one, and the other values add nothing, for 3 inversions.
figures.keyIdea: A smaller right value jumps over every left value still waiting.

figures.title: Four ways to walk a tree
figures.description: A binary search tree built from 8, 3, 10, 1, 6, 14, 4 and 7 has root 8, leaves 1, 4, 7 and 14, and height 3. Pre-order reads 8 3 1 6 4 7 10 14, in-order reads the keys sorted, post-order ends at the root 8, and level order reads one depth at a time.
figures.keyIdea: Pre, in and post order differ only in when the root is read.

figures.title: Delete with two children
figures.description: Deleting key 2 from a BinarySearchTree whose root 2 has children 1 and 4, with 3 below 4, copies the in-order successor 3 into the root and unlinks the old 3. The in-order keys become 1, 3, 4 and the height drops from 2 to 1.
figures.keyIdea: The successor's key replaces the deleted one; its old node is unlinked.

figures.title: Red links make 3-nodes
figures.description: After put 1 to 5, a RedBlackTreeMap has black root 4 with red left child 2, black children 1 and 3 under 2, and black 5. Read as a 2-3 tree it is the 3-node [2 4] over the 2-nodes [1], [3] and [5]; the height is 2 as a binary tree and 1 as a 2-3 tree.
figures.keyIdea: A red link and its black parent make one 3-node.

figures.title: Three local repairs
figures.description: Rotate left turns black 1 with a red right child 2 into black 2 with a red left child 1. Rotate right turns black 3 over red 2 over red 1 into black 2 with red children 1 and 3. Flip colors turns black 2 with red children into red 2 with black children.
figures.keyIdea: Rotations keep sorted order; a flip splits a 4-node.

figures.title: Linear search: first match
figures.description: linearSearch for 4 in 9, 4, 4, 2 inspects two cells and returns index 1, never reaching the second 4; a search for 7 inspects all four cells and returns -1.
figures.keyIdea: A hit stops the scan; only a miss costs n comparisons.

figures.title: Predicate boundary search
figures.description: For weights 3, 2, 2, 4, 1, 4 shipped in 3 days, capacities 4 and 5 are too slow and 6 to 16 fit. firstTrue(4, 17, fits) probes 10, 7, 5 and 6 and returns 6.
figures.keyIdea: Once a capacity fits, every larger one fits: each probe halves the range.

figures.title: Quickselect keeps one part
figures.description: kthSmallest of 7, 2, 9, 4, 4, 1 with k = 2: three partitions with pivots 7, 2 and 4 narrow the range from [0..5] to [0..3] to [2..3], and the equal part answers 4.
figures.keyIdea: k lies in one part of each partition: keep it, discard the rest.

figures.title: K-way merge with a heap
figures.description: mergeSorted of 1, 4, 7 and 2, 4 and 3, 6 keeps one head per list in a heap; when 4 from list A and 4 from list B tie, A pops first, giving 1, 2, 3, 4, 4, 6, 7.
figures.keyIdea: The smallest head is the next output; ties pop in list order.

figures.title: One insertion step
figures.description: In 3, 5, 8, 9, 4, 1 the prefix 3, 5, 8, 9 is sorted. The key 4 is saved, the three larger values 5, 8 and 9 shift one slot right, and 4 drops into index 1.
figures.keyIdea: Insertion sort shifts only the larger values one slot right, then drops the saved key into the gap, so the sorted prefix grows by one.

figures.title: Heapsort phases
figures.description: Heapsort on 3, 1, 6, 5, 2, 4 builds the max-heap 6, 5, 4, 1, 2, 3, then moves 6 and 5 to the end, giving 5, 3, 4, 1, 2, 6 and 4, 3, 2, 1, 5, 6, until 1 to 6 is sorted.
figures.keyIdea: Heapsort builds a max-heap, then swaps the root to the end and repairs the shorter heap; the sorted suffix grows by one each time.

figures.title: Counting sort tally
figures.description: For 5, 3, 6, 3, 4, 6 the range 3 to 6 has four counts: 2, 1, 1 and 2. Writing each value back that many times gives 3, 3, 4, 5, 6, 6.
figures.keyIdea: Counting sort never compares two values: it tallies each value, then writes each value back as many times as it was counted.

figures.title: Radix passes by digit
figures.description: Sorting 35, 21, 41, 15, 31, 25 by the ones digit gives 21, 41, 31, 35, 15, 25; a stable pass on the tens digit then gives 15, 21, 25, 31, 35, 41.
figures.keyIdea: Radix sort orders by the least significant digit first; because every pass is stable, ties keep the earlier order and the last pass leaves a full sort.

figures.title: Stable and unstable outcomes
figures.description: Records 3a, 1b, 3c, 2d, 1e, 3f sorted by their number: a stable sort gives 1b, 1e, 2d, 3a, 3c, 3f, keeping tags in order, while a hypothetical unstable outcome 1e, 1b, 2d, 3c, 3a, 3f reorders equal keys.
figures.keyIdea: A stable sort keeps equal keys in their input order; an unstable sort may reorder them, losing any earlier ordering by tag.

figures.title: Z-array and the Z-box
figures.description: The Z-array of aabxaabxaab is 11, 1, 0, 0, 7, 1, 0, 0, 3, 1, 0; the match at index 4 is a Z-box [4, 11), index 5 copies z[1] = 1 from it, and index 8 starts at 3 because z[4] = 7 overruns the box.
figures.keyIdea: z[i] starts from its mirror's value; only units past the box edge extend it.

figures.title: Rabin-Karp: hash, then verify
figures.description: Searching aeaecbagab for bagab slides a five-unit window; windows 0 and 5 have the pattern's hash, window 0 (aeaec) is rejected at unit 0 and window 5 is reported.
figures.keyIdea: Hash hits only choose where to compare; verification rejects impostors.

figures.title: Manacher: reuse the mirror
figures.description: In cabacabad the palindrome abacaba around index 4 spans [1, 7]; index 5 copies radius 1 from index 3 and index 6 caps radius 3 from index 2 at the 2 units left, giving odd radii 1, 1, 3, 1, 4, 1, 2, 1, 1.
figures.keyIdea: Inside a palindrome a center copies its mirror's radius, capped at the edge.

figures.title: Aho-Corasick links
figures.description: The trie of he, she, his and hers, then its failure links listed one per row: sh to h, she to he, his to s and hers to s; every other node links to the root.
figures.keyIdea: A failure link points at the longest suffix of a node that is still in the trie.

figures.title: Aho-Corasick scan
figures.description: Scanning ushers keeps the states root, s, sh, she, her and hers, and reports she at 1, he at 2 (through the link she to he) and hers at 2.
figures.keyIdea: One state per text unit; links report every pattern that ends at that unit.

figures.title: Suffix array and a pattern range
figures.description: The sorted suffixes of banana start at 5, 3, 1, 0, 4, 2 with lcp 0, 1, 3, 0, 0, 2; the pattern ana is the rank range [1, 3), whose starts 3 and 1 sort to 1, 3.
figures.keyIdea: Suffixes sharing a prefix sit side by side: a lookup is one range.
